Carried Out

label: text
text:
[From Our Own Correspondent.]
Canton June 29

label: text
text: General Chang... Kai-shek has some plan which puzzles even the most astute of Canton politicians.

label: text
text: Yesterday the acting chairman of the Executive Committee General Tan Yen-kai proposed that General Chang be made a member of the committee—the remaining important Government committee membership which the commander-in-chief did not hold. The motion was, of course, unanimously carried, as are all motions which concern Chang, or seem to have his approval.

label: text
text: Then Cheung Yan-kit, chairman of the Central Executive Committee of the Kuomintang took the chair and proposed, in view of the fact that General Chang Kai-shek will soon leave for the fighting front, that a special session of the entire Central Executive Committee be held for "special business" on July.

label: paragraph_title
text: Doing the Impossible.

label: text
text: This motion was unanimously carried, and telegrams were sent summoning all 36 members to be here on Sunday. Of course many of them will find it physically impossible to arrive here in time for the sessions, but most of those who will be unable to make the trip in the time specified are Lukewarm or hostile toward Chang Kai-shek, so the fact of their non-attendance will be immaterial.

label: text
text: It has been announced in advance that next Sunday's session will "concern governmental affairs," and that the results of the meeting will be kept secret.

label: text
text: The Nationalist Government yesterday appointed Tang Chak-yu to be the Central Executive Committee's representative on the board of directors of the $20,000,000 company "being organised to promote the development of" the Whampoa harbour. This selection displeases most of the Canton people, who had hoped to see Cantonese put in this place, instead of a Chekiang supporter of Chang Kai-shek.

label: paragraph_title
text: No More Conscription?

label: text
text: The Government's Northern expedition seems to be taking the form of a real determined push against Wu Pei-fu's allies at last. There are extensive military preparations of all kinds underway here, and the movement of troops northward has become a daily occurrence.

label: text
text: Alarmed by the indignation of the people against last week's conscription of coolies for service at the front, the Government has issued to the police and caused to be widely placarded a new order strictly forbidding further commandeering of coolies.

label: text
text: The term of service is announced as two or three months, and the wage will be $12 per month per man, with a rice allowance of $2.40 per month, and an additional 60 cents per month for straw sandals. The police are doubly cautioned that only volunteers may be accepted for this service.

label: paragraph_title
text: DOMINION DAY.

label: paragraph_title
text: OBSERVED BY CANADIAN COMMUNITY.

label: paragraph_title
text: TO-DAY'S TIFFIN.

label: text
text: To-day, Canadians all over the world celebrate the birthday of the Dominion—the accomplishment in 1867 of the federation of the various provinces under one Government—and the local Canadian community is not behind-hand with its observance.

label: text
text: A tiffin is being held at the Hongkong Hotel Roof Garden at 1 p.m. to-day at which it is hoped that H.E. the Governor, Sir Cecil Clementi, and other representative Government officials will be present. Some thirty members of the Canadian community will also be present.

label: text
text: Although the anniversary of Dominion Day is declared a public holiday by statute it coincides with the balancing by the Banks of the half yearly accounts—a double reason for the holiday which Hongkong is observing to-day.

label: paragraph_title
text: STILL SHOOTING.

label: text

PICKETS' CORDON AROUND.
H.K. ROAT.

label: text
text: GUNBOATS' VIGILANCE.

label: text
text:
[From Our Own Correspondent.]
Canton, June 29.

label: text
text: Every night for the last three nights there has been shooting around the Hongkong steamboat, when the pickets detect sampans trying to smuggle passengers or foodstuffs to the steamer. The gunboats in the river off Shameen take no part in these shooting affairs as long as they are confined to pickets and Chinese. They merely turn on their search lights, send boats to rescue the wounded, and then send the injured to hospitals in Canton, after giving them first aid on deck.

label: text
text: This recurrence of shooting is connected with the fact that the strike pickets, lenient for a time, are tightening their cordon. For a time the smuggling of passengers or goods, for a consideration, was easy, but so many pickets were caught making fat "squeeze" that the rules have been made more stringent.

label: text
text:
Customs "Row" Continues.
Because of the presence of several cases of suspected cholera in this vicinity, the Shameen authorities have circulated bulletins amongst the residents of the island.

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, Commander J. M. Kenworthy (Liberal, Central Hull) asked what docks in British territory in the Pacific were capable of accommodating the largest warships and what docks of such a size were being prepared in the Pacific besides those at Singapore?

label: text
text: After Mr. W. C. Bridgeman, First Lord of the Admiralty, had given the particulars requested Commander Kenworthy asked whether Mr. Bridgeman had considered with the Australian Government the enlargement of the dock accommodation at Sydney to enable it to take the largest ships?

label: text
text: Mr. Bridgeman replied that he was unable to say that he had done so recently, but he was unable, without notice, to say when the last communication occurred.

label: text
text: Mr. F. C. Penny (Conservative, Kingston-on-Thames) asked Mr. Bridgeman to consider the advisability of selling the Naval land and docks at Hongkong and devoting the proceeds to the building of the Singapore base.

label: text
text: The Speaker said that the question could not be answered without notice.—Reuter.

label: text
text: So serious has become the interference of union organisers and pickets with the employees of the Chinese Maritime Customs that sleeping quarters have been arranged within the Customs Building for many of the non-union employees who are terrorised and fear to go to their homes at night.

label: text
text: Once more the unions have defied the law. Yesterday, the owners of tea-houses and restaurants—the employees of which have been on strike—met to organise an owners' guild, and to determine upon steps to take to break the strike. However, strikers surrounded the building in which the meeting was held, and with loud cries demanded the surrender of the five leaders of the opposition. They boldly said they meant to take these opponents away and kill them.

label: text
text: The restaurant owners, in panic, telephoned to police station No. 3, but not until two bodies of police reserves had been sent to the scene would the strikers disperse.

label: text
text: EXECUTIVE'S DECISION

label: text
text: The Mirers' Federation Executive met for these hours and discussed among other matters the question of withdrawing safety men from the pit of consequences of complaints of colliery managers violating local agreements.

label: text
text: The Executive decided at present to adhere to their decision to allow safety men to continue, as their withdrawal would unfairly penalise those collier companies loyally observing the agreement. — Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text:
Labour Threat.
London June 30

label: text
text: In the House of Commons, on the Committee of the Coal Mines Bill, Mr. Bensuy MacDonald said that the Labourites regarded the measure too bad in principle for them to attempt an amendment. The Labourites would wipe it off the Statute-Book at the first opportunity.

label: text
text: The only amendment was submitted by the Labourite, Captain Wedgwood Benn, proposing to insert a provision that the Bill might be suspended or repealed by a resolution of both Houses. Captain Benn said that foreign countries were closely watching such legislation. He did not wish the measure to start international competition and sweating.

label: text
text: The amendment was defeated, the division resulting: Against

label: text
text:
Majority.....205
The Labourites abstained from voting.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: Closure Applied

label: text
text: The House of Commons concluded the Committee stage of the Coal Mines Bill of Law is a lengthy debate in which the government applied the closure and secured majorities ranging from 135 to 139 on the main clauses of the Bill.

label: paragraph_title
text: A DANGER.

label: paragraph_title
text: Lowering Standard of Living.

label: text
text: In the Committee stage of the Bill, providing for an eight-hour day in mines, Captain Wedgwood, Benn (Liberal), moved an amendment providing that the operation of the Bill could be repealed or suspended at any time by a resolution of both Houses of Parliament. He declared that while the prescribed term of the operation of the Bill was five years, it was practically permanent. Legislation of this kind was being watched very carefully abroad. The danger which the Coal Commission foresaw—that the lowering of the standard in our land would result in the comparative lowering of standard in other countries—was well grounded. Whether we took Switzerland, Poland, Germany, or Italy, everywhere they would find that this sort of attack was being made on hours of labour and the standard of living.

label: paragraph_title
text: Remedy Simple.

label: text
text: Sir Arthur Steel Maitland, Minister of Labour, in resisting the amendment, declared that if the grave contingency contemplated by Captain Wedgwood Benn occurred the Government of the day could easily (as had been done on many previous occasions) remedy the situation by legislation. Amending, repealing, or suspending could be passed at once. He did not for a moment anticipate that such an event would ever occur. Moreover, what was required for some time was that agreements should be made of lasting duration.

label: text
text: The Miners Executive considered the question of withdrawing safety question of withdrawing safety men from the pits. They decided, in the words of a statement issued afterward, not to interfere with safety workers "unless their presence in minea is abused." Some of the miners leaders say that the owners have broken the agreements in regard to safety men and that other use is being made of a co intended only for colliery boilers. The owners deny that there has been any such breaches of agreement.

label: text
text: In the House of Commons Minister of Labour said that the amount lost in wages during the general strike was estimated at $500,000,000 and $16,000,000. — British Wireless Service

label: text
text: After five years the Rents Restriction Ordinance is to-day, a thing of the past, having lapsed yesterday, as notified previously by the Government.

label: text
text: It was on July 1, 1921, that the Ordinance came into force, with the rental on December 31, 1920, as the standard figure. Subsequently the law was amended when necessary and landlords were allowed a 15 per cent increase twelve months ago.

His view was that premises, on which rents were unduly low, would now be marketable, so that there would be a steady flow of transactions. The non-restriction of development also counted for a good deal, said Mr. Lam.

label: text
text:
At the annual reception of the Royal Colonial Institute H.R.H. the Prince of Wales presented the gold medal of the Institute for the best book relating to the Empire to Sir Federick Lugard (Governor of Hongkong from 1907 to 1912) for his book entitled "Our Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa."
The Prince of Wales paid a tribute to Sir F. Lugard as a fin Governor and a great Colonial Civil Servant.

label: text
text: As the outcome of inquiries made yesterday by the “Kung Sheung Yat Po.” it was found that in five or six instances, tenants of shop premises in or near the Chinese business, centre had been approached by landlords for increases of rent, ranging from $15 to $30 or $40 per month. This was not considered unreasonable. Owners of fairly large lots of property, says the same vernacular paper, have not made any signs of a move toward higher rents, possibly on account of depressed conditions.

label: text
text: From banking sources, the "China Mall" learned that money — for investment in property— is fairly cheap and plentiful at the moment. Rates of from 8½ to 9 per cent per annum are obtainable by buyers of houses, who wish to obtain a mortgage up to half (or over) the amount required. Terms of loans (on those rates of interest) are generally for a year, with possible extensions.

label: paragraph_title
text: MOTOR FATALITY

label: text
text: A Chinese girl, about six years old, was knocked down by a motor car shortly after 7 p.m. yesterday and died almost immediately.

label: text
text: The car, which is reported as belonging to Mr. Nemazee and driven by the chauffeur, apparently swerved in Robinson Road, near the Roman Catholic Cathedral, in order to avoid a number of children playing on the road and, in doing so, struck the girl down.

label: paragraph_title
text: BULLET EXTRACTED.

label: text
text: The passer-by who was wounded in the shooting, affray, near the Central Market on Sunday, night has had a bullet removed from his right thigh, after treatment in the Government Civil Hospital.

label: paragraph_title
text: PIRATES' PROFITS.

label: text
text: GANG EARNING $100,000 A

label: text
text: A pirate's agent is suspected of being in the Colony at the moment to purchase two steam launches for his master's "Navy."

label: text
text:
The pirate chief is believed to be the one who cut off an easy from each of about 70 strike pickets who fell into his hands after bad blood about his alleged amuggling of foreign cargo. As reprisal, regular troops were sent and his den has been wiped out. Over 20 victims in captivity (from whom the outlaw had expected ransom) were released and the pirate lost arms and ammunition valued at over $20,000. The balance of his arsenal is concealed in the hills.
This gang is estimated to be "earning" over $100,000 a year in tolls from communities and traders who pay them protection fees and safe conduct money. Until the force is fitted out again, the majority of its members are having a holiday.
Then, again, another notorious pirate captain is reported to contemplate retirement in Shanghai to spend his old days in peace with his seven or eight wives and incidentally, his ill-cotten fortune of half a million dollars.
Shortly after his kit fast wife died last year, this bandit took unto himself a tin long to whom is attributed this sudden desire to lead a life of comfort. The gang thrived around the East River until dispersed by a Canton punitive expedition.
Misfortune overtook the chief, taller after his defeat in the field by the military. His brother is posted as missing and his father was captured. With only $200 the leader stole away in disguise, using a small campan. He was followed by a clansman. This chinsman actually told "he pirate that he had all his life swaggered down on unoffending people and asked for "loans." Now it was his (the clansman's) turn and he wanted a "loan" of $5,000 from the robber. The latter still had his wits with him. Asking his clansman to return the next day he immediately fled to Shanghai, and his herom is now reported as being on the way to join him.

label: text
text:
Such is fame! A copy of the "China Mail" 50 years old has been sent to the London "Evening News" by a veader, after a reference to the Seven Seas Club.
In "the Diary of a Man About Town" (Evening News of May 28, 1926) appears the following:

label: text
text: Like a breath from the sea that we read about in the old days comes this letter, and see how plainly and clearly a sailorman can write! It comes to me (says the Man About Town) from a Mr. George Warr, who lives in London, S.W.

label: text
text:
"I am sending this copy of the China Mail," he writes, "as I think it might be interesting to some of your friends of the Seven Seas Club whom you write about in The Evening News. I don't know if it is of any value as a curlo."
"I was a stoker in the Navy in 1894, and my first ship was the Immortalite (Captain Sir Edward Chichester), and we served four years on the China Station, and when I read your article about the Club and Hong Kong I thought about this old paper I had had all these years in my old ditty box."

label: text
text:
"You will see by the date that it is close on 50 years old. I think it is interesting as showing how rapid was the change from sail to steam in those 20 years from 1870 to 1890, because you will notice that every one of the ships in the 'Shipping' carries full sail, whether steamship or only sailing ship, whereas when we went out there to Hong Kong in the beginning of 1895 it was the exception to see any sailing ship at all. They were all steam.
"I hope you will excuse this letter; writing is not my strong point."
